Advanced Packaging, stage 11 of 15Next stage: 12 Substrates and PCBs

ConcentrationExtremeHigh

In plain terms

Packaging joins finished chips into one component and mounts them on a small circuit board, called a substrate, wired far more coarsely than the chips themselves. A lithography machine, which prints a chip's circuits, can cover only a rectangle about the size of a postage stamp in one shot. Many leading accelerators, Nvidia's Blackwell among them, need more logic than fits in that rectangle. So they are built from several chips, called dies, set side by side on an interposer, a layer of much finer wiring that links them and sits on the substrate. Stacks of memory chips sit on the same interposer, a few millimeters away. The interposer is either one piece of silicon or layers of fine copper wiring that often carry small silicon bridges where the links are densest. Silicon expands less than the resin substrate beneath it when heated, so the package can warp and its joints crack. Preventing that in high volume is hard. Nvidia, Google, AMD and Amazon all use TSMC's interposer packaging, called CoWoS, made in Taiwan.

In short

Epoch AI estimates that in 2025 Nvidia used 60.3 percent of all capacity for CoWoS, TSMC's interposer packaging[1]. On the July 2026 earnings call, TSMC's chief executive, C.C. Wei, said its packaging capacity was so tight that it limited customers' growth[2]. Asked about Intel's EMIB-T packaging, he said he hoped it would take some of the load off TSMC[2].

In a TrendForce ranking by 2024 revenue, which CSET cites, four of the top ten outsourced firms that package and test chips are headquartered in China[3]. But in 2025 Chinese firms had 5.3 percent of the market for advanced packaging fabrication tools, against 65.8 percent for US firms, by CSET's analysis of TechInsights data[4].

Why substitution is possible
CoWoS packaging has been outsourced to assembly firms such as ASE and Amkor before[11]. Intel's EMIB, which links chips through silicon bridges embedded in the substrate, is another option, and Amazon's Trainium and Google's TPU were both adopting it as of March 2026[11]. But a newcomer would have to match TSMC, which said in April 2026 that it was producing CoWoS at 5.5 times the area a scanner prints in one shot[12].
Where China stands

Chinese firms had 5.3 percent of the market for fabrication tools built for advanced packaging in 2025, by CSET's analysis of TechInsights data[4]. Between 2019 and 2024 they gained 5 percentage points of share in test tools but lost share in bonding and other conventional assembly and packaging tools[3].

Where the US stands

Intel opened Fab 9 in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, in January 2024 to make its Foveros 3D packages in volume[6]. Amkor broke ground in October 2025 on a $7B packaging and test campus in Peoria, Arizona, and expects production to start in early 2028[13].

Specimen · CoWoS package, exploded

A CoWoS-L package, pulled apart. Two logic dies and eight HBM stacks sit on the interposer, shown in silver with its copper wiring. In CoWoS-L the interposer is fine redistribution wiring with small embedded silicon bridges. It sits on a resin substrate with a grid of solder balls underneath. The chips together cover about 2,700 mm2, a little over three reticle fields. Footprints are to scale. Thicknesses and the gaps between layers are exaggerated.

See it in 3D in the interactive chapter

A lithography scanner prints a rectangle 26 mm by 33 mm, or 858 mm2, in one exposure[14]. That area is called the reticle field. Every leading AI accelerator, counting its memory stacks, covers more area than that. Packaging is the stage that lets an accelerator be larger than one reticle field, and the packaging method limits how much larger it can be.

How it works

A second reason for the interposer is high bandwidth memory (HBM). An HBM4 stack connects through 2,048 data signals, packed too tightly for a standard resin substrate, so the memory sits beside the logic on the interposer[15]. Even Nvidia's H100, whose single logic die is 814 mm2 and fits inside one reticle field, carries five HBM stacks[16]. Epoch AI counts TSMC's CoWoS packaging among the three inputs the H100 needs, along with its logic die and its HBM[1].

CoWoS stands for chip on wafer on substrate, the order in which the parts are joined. For CoWoS-S, the version whose interposer is one piece of silicon, TSMC makes a silicon wafer that carries wiring and vertical copper vias but no transistors. Vias are metal-filled holes that join one layer of wiring to the next.

TSMC bonds the logic dies and memory stacks face down onto that wafer with microbumps. These are dots of solder, and each dot is one electrical joint. In Intel's Foveros 2.5D packaging, which can also set dies side by side on a silicon interposer, the microbumps sit 36 micrometers apart, less than half a hair's width[17]. Then TSMC cuts the interposer out of the wafer and attaches it to the resin substrate, which later goes onto a circuit board.

One cracked joint can scrap a package holding eight tested HBM stacks and two large, expensive logic dies. Epoch AI estimated in December 2025 that CoWoS-L packaging, the version built with small silicon bridges, added about $1,100 to the cost of building one Nvidia B200[5]. That is more than its estimate of about $900 for the B200's two logic dies[5].

2.5D: silicon, RDL and bridges

In 2.5D packaging the chips sit side by side and connect through an interposer or silicon bridges beneath them. TSMC has run CoWoS in volume since 2012[18]. CoWoS-S has the finest wiring, but its interposer is one unbroken piece of silicon whose yield (the share of interposers that work) falls as the area grows. CoWoS-L replaces that piece of silicon with redistribution layers (RDL) of fine copper wiring and embeds small silicon bridges where the wiring is densest[19].

Intel's EMIB embeds similar silicon bridges in the resin substrate[17]. SemiAnalysis reported in March 2026 that EMIB was gaining traction, with Amazon's Trainium and Google's TPU both adopting it[11].

Blackwell was the first high-volume design on CoWoS-L, and packaging problems at TSMC and in Nvidia's design limited its supply[20]. The bridges that carry the 10 TB/s link between the two logic dies must be placed very precisely[20]. The dies, bridges, interposer and substrate also expand at different rates, and that mismatch caused warpage[20].

3D: SoIC and Foveros

In 3D packaging one die sits on top of another, and the joints between them are moving from solder microbumps to hybrid bonding. Intel's Foveros stacks dies face to face and joins them with solder microbumps[17]. Its newer Foveros Direct drops the solder and bonds the copper pads directly, a method called hybrid bonding[17]. Hybrid bonding joins the insulating layer around the pads as well as the copper, with no bumps in between[21]. That lets the connections sit far closer together than microbumps allow[17]. TSMC's SoIC also uses hybrid bonding, and AMD's 3D V-Cache processors use SoIC to attach an extra cache die to the processor die[22].

TSMC put SoIC into volume production in 2022, stacking SRAM memory chips on logic wafers[23]. Its 3 nm SoIC entered volume production in 2025[19]. An A14-on-A14 version, stacking dies made on TSMC's 1.4 nm process, is due in 2029[12]. It will carry 1.8 times the die-to-die connection density of SoIC that stacks 2 nm dies on 2 nm dies[12].

In a stack the bottom die is the hardest to cool and the top die is the hardest to power. Because of the heat, 3D designs often put cache memory underneath and compute circuits on top.

SoIC bonding also brings optics into the package. TSMC's COUPE uses SoIC to join a silicon photonics chip, which sends data as light, to its electrical control chip[19]. TSMC said in April 2026 that COUPE on substrate would begin production in 2026[12]. It also said that putting COUPE inside the package gives twice the power efficiency of a pluggable version on the circuit board[12].

Two ways off the silicon interposer

Panel-level packaging builds packages on a large rectangular panel instead of a round wafer, so rectangular packages fit it with less waste at the edges. See Test and assembly. JEDEC, the semiconductor standards body, published a standard called SPHBM4 on 13 July 2026. It puts HBM4 memory on a base chip carrying 512 data signals instead of 2,048, each running four times as fast to keep the same bandwidth[15]. With fewer signals, the connections can be spaced widely enough to mount the stack on a standard resin substrate instead of the silicon interposer[15].

Capacity

TSMC does not publish its CoWoS capacity[1]. Industry estimates from SemiWiki and TrendForce, compiled by Epoch AI, put it at about 65,000 to 75,000 wafers a month at the end of 2025, up from 35,000 to 40,000 a year earlier[1].

In 2024 TSMC was more than doubling CoWoS capacity and still could not keep up with demand. On the July 2024 earnings call, TSMC's chief executive, C.C. Wei, said TSMC was more than doubling CoWoS capacity in 2024 and would more than double it again in 2025[24]. He said he could not yet balance supply and demand[24]. At its 2024 symposium TSMC had said CoWoS capacity would grow at a 60 percent compound annual rate over the next few years[24]. Asked about that rate on the call, Wei did not repeat it[24].

In October 2025 Wei would say only that TSMC was still working to increase CoWoS capacity in 2026, and that it would probably give the actual capacity figure in 2026[25]. He said front-end capacity (making the chips) and back-end capacity (packaging them) were both, in his words, very tight[25].

By Epoch AI's estimate, four chip designers used most of the world's CoWoS capacity in 2025 but only a small share of its advanced chipmaking. Epoch AI compared each chip designer's use of components with world supply[1]. It puts Nvidia at 60.3 percent of all CoWoS capacity in 2025, with a 90 percent confidence interval of 56.5 to 64.3[1]. Google took 13.5 percent, AMD 8.4 and Amazon 7.4[1]. Together those four used around 90 percent of global CoWoS capacity and HBM supply, with HBM measured by value[1]. But they used only 12 percent of advanced logic die production[1].

In March 2026 the research firm SemiAnalysis judged that front-end capacity had become the dominant bottleneck and that CoWoS constraints were easing[11]. It said TSMC was planning CoWoS capacity around how many wafers N3, its 3 nm process, could produce, because added packaging capacity is of no use without front-end wafers to fill it[11]. It also noted that CoWoS packaging can be, and has been, outsourced to assembly firms such as ASE and Amkor[11].

TSMC gave a different account four months later. On the July 2026 earnings call, Wei said TSMC's packaging capacity was so tight that it limited customers' growth[2]. Asked about Intel's EMIB-T, he said he welcomed the extra flexibility and hoped it would take some of the load off TSMC[2]. Later in the call he said back-end capacity was still in shortage[26].

Who makes it

Three kinds of firm package chips. TSMC, which makes chips for others, and Intel, which makes its own, do it in their own back-end fabs. Outsourced assembly and test firms do the rest. Intel opened Fab 9 in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, in January 2024 to make its Foveros 3D packages in volume[6]. It called the plant the only US factory producing the most advanced packaging at scale[6].

ASE leads the outsourced assembly and test firms, and Amkor is the largest one headquartered in the United States. ASE Technology Holding had revenue of NT$645.4 billion in 2025, about 40 percent of it from its electronics manufacturing arm, a business separate from assembly and test[7]. Its assembly, test and materials business brought in NT$389.2 billion, up from NT$325.9 billion in 2024[7]. Amkor had net sales of $6.71 billion in 2025[8].

Each of the key packaging tools comes from a small number of makers.

  • Thermocompression bonding. Pressing dies together under heat and force. ASMPT's advanced packaging revenue reached $532.1 million in 2025, with thermocompression bonder revenue up about 146 percent[10]. ASMPT targets 35 to 40 percent of a market it puts at $1.6 billion in 2028[10].
  • Hybrid bonding. Copper pads and the insulator around them bond directly, with no solder. Applied Materials co-developed its Kinex hybrid bonding system with Besi, which Applied calls the industry leader in hybrid bonding[27].
  • Grinding and dicing. Disco held 87 percent of the $1.9 billion world market for dicing tools in 2025, by CSET's count from TechInsights data[28]. The category covers the grinders that thin wafers and the saws that cut them into chips[28]. See Test and assembly.

TSMC and Amkor both plan advanced packaging plants in Arizona. TSMC's Arizona commitment reached $265 billion in July 2026 and covers two advanced packaging plants alongside 10 fabs[29]. Amkor started building a $7 billion campus in Peoria, Arizona, in October 2025 and expects production from early 2028[13]. The US Commerce Department awarded Amkor up to $407 million in CHIPS Act funding for the site in December 2024[30]. In October 2025 Wei said a large outsourced packaging partner, which he did not name, was already breaking ground in Arizona[31]. He said its plant was on an earlier schedule than TSMC's own two packaging fabs there[31].

The chokepoint

Four of the top ten outsourced assembly and test firms by 2024 revenue are headquartered in China, by a TrendForce ranking that CSET cites[3]. JCET, a leading Chinese assembly and test firm, had record revenue of RMB 38.87 billion in 2025, up 8.1 percent[9]. JCET says its XDFOI packaging platform has entered high-volume manufacturing with redistribution-layer interposer, silicon interposer and silicon bridge options[32]. Those are the same three kinds of carrier that TSMC sells as CoWoS-R, CoWoS-S and CoWoS-L.

Chinese firms had a small share of the market for advanced packaging tools in 2024 and 2025, and they lost ground in bonding. In 2024 Chinese firms had 7 percent of the market for advanced packaging fabrication tools[3]. Between 2019 and 2024, they gained 5 percentage points of share in test tools and 4 points in fabrication tools built for advanced packaging, by CSET's analysis of TechInsights data[3]. But they lost share in bonding and other conventional assembly and packaging tools, the category where CSET counts hybrid and thermocompression bonders[3]. Within the advanced packaging fabrication tools, Chinese firms gained 10 points in etch and clean tools and 3 points in deposition tools[3]. They lost 2 points each in lithography and polishing (CMP) tools[3]. CSET's Chip Explorer, a separate data tool also built on TechInsights data, puts Chinese firms at 5.3 percent of the $6.2 billion world market for advanced packaging fabrication tools in 2025[4]. It puts US firms at 65.8 percent and Japanese firms at 15.3 percent[4].

TSMC said in April 2026 that it was producing CoWoS at 5.5 times the size of a reticle field and planning larger versions[12]. Each generation on TSMC's roadmap needs a larger interposer.

  • 2028. A 14-reticle interposer, about the area of a compact disc, carrying about ten large compute dies and 20 HBM stacks[12].
  • 2029. More than 14 reticles, plus a 40-reticle System-on-Wafer[12]. TSMC describes System-on-Wafer as joining different data center chips at the scale of a whole wafer[33].

Review questions

Open a question to see its answer.

Why is an AI accelerator built from several chips in one package?

Many leading accelerators, Nvidia's Blackwell among them, need more logic than a lithography machine can print in one shot.

Packaging sets the chips and their memory side by side on an interposer, a shared wiring layer, and wires them together through it. Even the H100, built as one chip, uses an interposer to connect its memory. Reread: How it works

Which company do Nvidia, Google, AMD and Amazon rely on to package their AI accelerators?

TSMC, in Taiwan.

TSMC's packaging process is called CoWoS. Nvidia alone took an estimated 60.3 percent of CoWoS capacity in 2025. Reread: Who makes it

Why has packaging limited how many AI chips can be made?

TSMC could not add CoWoS capacity fast enough to meet demand, even while more than doubling it in 2024.

Packaging problems on CoWoS-L also limited the supply of Nvidia's Blackwell, the first high-volume design to use it. In July 2026 TSMC said its packaging capacity was still so tight that it limited customers' growth. Reread: Capacity

Where are advanced chip packages made in volume in the United States?

At Intel's Fab 9 in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, which makes Intel's Foveros 3D packages.

Intel calls it the only US factory producing the most advanced packaging at scale. Amkor expects its packaging plant in Peoria, Arizona, to start production in early 2028. Reread: Who makes it
